stops.name: Beit Nuba, the shield before Jerusalem
stops.campa: A second advance brings the army back to Beit Nuba in June, and this time the French and English captains fall out openly: Hugh of Burgundy and the French will have a siege of Jerusalem outright; Richard argues, against his own evident wish, that the army lacks strength to hold what it might take, and that Egypt, not Jerusalem, is the sultan's real spine to break. Riding out on patrol, he comes to a hilltop from which the city itself is visible for the first time, and, the legend tells, will not look: he raises his shield before his eyes, saying he is not worthy to see the city he cannot deliver.

stops.name: Jaffa, the battle and the King's last charge
stops.campa: Saladin strikes at Jaffa while Richard is still at Acre, and the town falls before Richard's galleys can beat down the coast; landing at speed with a handful of knights, Richard wades ashore through the surf, drives the garrison of Saladin's men still looting the town back out through the gates, and holds the ruined walls with barely enough men to be called a garrison. Days later Saladin's whole army tries again in the open field before the town; Richard, on a borrowed horse, charges the Muslim line so far ahead of his own knights that Saladin himself, watching, sends him a fresh mount rather than see so brave a man unhorsed and killed by chance.

stops.name: Jaffa, the treaty and the pilgrims allowed
stops.campa: Both sides are spent. On the second of September Richard and Saladin conclude, through al-Adil, the Treaty of Jaffa: a three-year truce, Jerusalem to remain in Muslim hands but open to unarmed Christian pilgrims, a strip of coast from Tyre to Jaffa left to the Franks. Richard himself, ill again and unwilling to enter the city he cannot hold as a conqueror, does not make the pilgrimage; his soldiers go up to the Holy Sepulchre in parties under safe-conduct while their king remains on the coast. He is remembered as swearing he would return and finish what this crusade left undone. He never does.
stops.quote: If the land were to be lost in his time, he would rather have it taken into Richard's mighty power than see it go into the hands of any other prince he had ever seen.
stops.quote_source: Saladin's reply to Richard's truce embassy, Itinerarium Peregrinorum et Gesta Regis Ricardi, reported under late July 1192, in the negotiations that ended in the Treaty of Jaffa

stops.name: Acre, the departure
stops.campa: On the ninth of October Richard sails from Acre for home, word having reached him that Philip Augustus is conspiring with his brother John against the Angevin lands he has left ungoverned for three years. He leaves the crusade's work half finished and its army dispersed to a dozen quarrels over who will rule what remains of the kingdom of Jerusalem. The chroniclers give him a last look back at the coastline: he is said to pray, as the sails fill, that God grant him to return one day and see the Holy City again. Instead it is the last time in his life he sees the Levant.

stops.name: Corfu, the pirate galleys
stops.campa: The fleet, wary of the ports of southern Italy and Sicily where Richard has enemies, works its way up the Adriatic; off Corfu, on the eleventh of November, Richard's ship falls in with a pair of pirate galleys. Rather than fight or flee them he hires them outright — the fastest, most anonymous vessels he can find for a passage he already knows must be made quietly, by a route no one expects a crusading king to take. He travels now with only a handful of companions, his own fleet sent ahead or scattered: a king trying to vanish into the sea he has just conquered a kingdom's worth of enemies upon.

stops.name: Aquileia, the wreck and the landfall
stops.campa: A storm in the small hours of the second and third of December drives the hired galleys onto the coast near Aquileia, at the head of the Adriatic — deep inside territory hostile to him on every side, ringed by lords loyal to the Emperor Henry VI or to the kin of his own crusade-enemy Conrad of Montferrat. Richard comes ashore with a handful of men, disguises himself as a merchant pilgrim — some say as a Knight Templar — and resolves to strike overland through the mountains for his brother-in-law's lands in Saxony rather than risk the open roads of Italy, where his own name is a death warrant.

stops.name: Friesach, the ride in disguise
stops.campa: For nineteen days Richard rides north and east through Carinthia and lower Austria with only William de l'Étang and a German-speaking boy for company, posing as a merchant returning from pilgrimage, paying too freely for a poor man and giving himself away by wearing, under his rough cloak, a jewelled ring he cannot bring himself to sell. At the hardest stretch they cover some hundred and fifty miles in three days, sleeping little, eating worse, twice nearly taken at inns where local lords grow suspicious of a traveller who will not give his name and pays in gold no merchant carries.

stops.name: Vienna, Erdberg, the capture
stops.campa: Fifty miles short of the Moravian border and safety, sick with fever and unable to ride further, Richard stops to rest at an inn in Erdberg, a suburb of Vienna, sending the boy into the market for provisions and, fatally, to change money too freely for a servant's purse. The boy is stopped, questioned, and under pressure names his master; Leopold of Austria's men surround the inn. Richard is found in the kitchen, it is said, turning a spit, and refuses to yield his sword to any but the Duke himself. Leopold comes in person: the man whose banner was thrown in the ditch at Acre now holds the King of England prisoner.

stops.name: Dürnstein, the castle on the Danube
stops.campa: Leopold holds his prize secretly at first, then openly, in the castle of Dürnstein above a bend of the Danube, guarded by the castellan Hadmar von Kuenring. News of an English king vanished on the road home spreads through Europe faster than any confirmed report of where he is; a later and much-loved legend fills the gap with the minstrel Blondel de Nesle, wandering castle to castle singing the first half of a song only he and Richard know, until from behind Dürnstein's wall a voice takes up the second verse. In truth the Emperor has already written to announce the capture. The legend outlives the correction.

stops.name: Speyer, brought before the Emperor
stops.campa: Leopold surrenders his prisoner to the Emperor Henry VI, who nurses larger grievances against Richard — old quarrels over Sicily and Tancred, and Richard's friendship with Henry's rival for that crown. Brought before the imperial Diet at Speyer, formally accused of conspiring against the Emperor's cousin and of the murder of Conrad of Montferrat, Richard defends himself alone, without counsel, in a speech the chroniclers say moves hardened enemies to tears — regal, unbroken, as though he sat on his own throne at Lincoln or Caen. He is not acquitted, but the mood of the hall turns, and the Emperor shifts from trial toward the arithmetic of ransom.

stops.name: Trifels, the fortress and the prison song
stops.campa: Moved to Trifels castle in the Rhineland hills, held under harsher watch than Dürnstein's, Richard composes — in French and in the langue d'oc together, the two tongues of his mother's court — a song addressed to his half-sister Marie of Champagne: Ja nus hons pris ne dira sa raison, no man who is imprisoned can tell his case aright, save sorrowfully. He complains not of chains but of a slower cruelty: two winters gone and no lord or kinsman come to ransom him, while lesser men are freed for less. It is the truest surviving record of his own voice, spoken in the one tongue captivity cannot take from a poet's son.
stops.quote: Ja nus hons pris ne dira sa raison / Adroitement, se dolantement non; / Mais par confort puet il faire chançon. / Assez ai d'amis, mais povre sont li don; / Honte i avront, se por ma reançon / Sui ça deux yvers pris.
stops.quote_source: "Ja nus hons pris" (RS 1891), composed by Richard I in captivity, 1193 — text normalized from the chansonnier tradition; the place is given variously as Dürnstein or Trifels

stops.name: Worms, the ransom set
stops.campa: The Emperor and his council set the price of the King of England's freedom at one hundred and fifty thousand marks of silver — some three times the annual revenue of the whole English crown — to be paid before Richard is released, with hostages of high rank held against the balance. Word crosses to England within weeks. Eleanor of Aquitaine, seventy years old and regent again in her son's absence as she was once in her husband's, begins stripping the kingdom for it: a quarter of every man's income and goods, the gold and silver plate of the churches, scutage on every knight's fee, wool sold off the sheep's back before shearing.
